1	(* FlatArrays -- the array vocabulary of Run C4: what the shipped
2	   Vector/Matrix algebra lacks, declared once in the library's own style over
3	   the library's own arrays.  Round two's vocabulary (explorations/run-c/src)
4	   less the block, ravel, vector-gather and validity pieces that the corpus
5	   object of FlatData makes unnecessary; the inventory it was built against
6	   is round three's survey (explorations/run-c3/survey.md).  Views take their
7	   shapes at run time through the library's own reflect idiom
8	   (FortressLibrary.fss:1922-1934). *)
9	component FlatArrays
10	export FlatArrays
11	import NatReflect.{...}
12	
13	(* ------------------------------------------------------- constructors ---- *)
14	vec(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> RR64): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).tabulate(f)
15	zeros(n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(0.0)
16	keys(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> ZZ32): Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] = array[\ZZ32\](n).tabulate(f)
17	mat(r: ZZ32, c: ZZ32, f: (ZZ32,ZZ32) -> RR64): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = array[\RR64\](r,c).tabulate(f)
18	
19	(* ------------------------------------------- the elementwise algebra ----- *)
20	(* One declaration per operator, generic in the index type I, so a vector
21	   (I = ZZ32), a matrix ((ZZ32,ZZ32)) and a rank-3 array share it.  A scalar
22	   times an array is the library's juxtaposition and is not redeclared;
23	   + and - between two arrays of one shape, and + - MIN MAX between an array
24	   and a scalar, are the library's. *)
25	opr ×[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], b: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (i: I, e: RR64): RR64 => e b[i])
26	opr /[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], b: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (i: I, e: RR64): RR64 => e / b[i])
27	opr /[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => e / s)
28	(* a comparison on an array is a 0/1 array *)
29	opr >[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => if e > s then 1.0 else 0.0 end)
30	opr SQRT[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => SQRT e)
31	exp[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => exp(e))
32	log[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => log(e))
33	(* diag(v) m scales the rows of m: the Dyalog's v ×⍤0 1 m.  A diagonal is a
34	   read-only Matrix view; the library's product forwards to its mul, which
35	   scales the rows without forming the matrix. *)
36	object Diag[\nat s\](d: Vector[\RR64,s\]) extends Matrix[\RR64,s,s\]
37	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; if i = j then d[i] else 0.0 end end
38	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = fail("a diagonal is read-only")
39	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = fail("a diagonal is read-only")
40	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,s,0,s\] = array2[\U,s,s\]()
41	    mul[\nat s2\](other: Matrix[\RR64,s,s2\]): Matrix[\RR64,s,s2\] =
42	        other.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), e: RR64): RR64 => do (i, j) = ij; d[i] e end)
43	end
44	diag[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Diag[\s\] = Diag[\s\](v)
45	
46	(* ----------------------------------------------------- transposes -------- *)
47	(* as functions, and as ^T over them *)
48	transpose[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = m.t()
49	transpose[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]): Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = Transposed3[\a,b,c\](t)
50	opr (m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\])^T[\nat r, nat c\]: Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = transpose(m)
51	opr (t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\])^T[\nat a, nat b, nat c\]: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = transpose(t)
52	
53	(* ------------------------------------------------------------ views ----- *)
54	(* the (nr x nc) matrix at off in a flat vector, row-major *)
55	object PView[\nat s, nat r, nat c\](base: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32) extends Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]
56	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get(off + i c + j) end
57	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put(off + i c + j, x) end
58	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0(off + i c + j, x) end
59	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,r,0,c\] = array2[\U,r,c\]()
60	end
61	viewN[\nat s, nat r, nat c\](base: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32, _: N[\r\], _: N[\c\]): Matrix[\RR64,r,c\] =
62	    PView[\s,r,c\](base, off)
63	view[\nat s\](p: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32, nr: ZZ32, nc: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
64	    viewN(p, off, reflect(nr), reflect(nc))
65	
66	(* a row of a matrix, and a row of a plane of a rank-3 array, as a Vector *)
67	object RowView[\nat r, nat c\](base: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], i: ZZ32) extends Vector[\RR64,c\]
68	    get(j: ZZ32): RR64 = base.get(i, j)
69	    put(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.put((i, j), x)
70	    init0(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.init0((i, j), x)
71	    replica[\U\](): Array1[\U,0,c\] = array1[\U,c\]()
72	end
73	row[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = RowView[\r,c\](m, i)
74	object Row3View[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32, i: ZZ32) extends Vector[\RR64,c\]
75	    get(j: ZZ32): RR64 = base.get((p, i, j))
76	    put(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.put((p, i, j), x)
77	    init0(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.init0((p, i, j), x)
78	    replica[\U\](): Array1[\U,0,c\] = array1[\U,c\]()
79	end
80	row3[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32, i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = Row3View[\a,b,c\](t, p, i)
81	
82	(* a (docs.positions x heads.dim) activation as docs.heads planes of positions x dim:
83	   plane d nh + h, row i, column j is base[d p + i, h k + j]; and the inverse *)
84	object HeadsView[\nat br, nat bc, nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Matrix[\RR64,br,bc\], p: ZZ32, nh: ZZ32, k: ZZ32)
85	        extends Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]
86	    get(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (q, i, j) = ix; base.get((q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j) end
87	    put(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (q, i, j) = ix; base.put(((q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j), x) end
88	    init0(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (q, i, j) = ix; base.init0(((q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j), x) end
89	    replica[\U\](): Array3[\U,0,a,0,b,0,c\] = array3[\U,a,b,c\]()
90	end
91	headsN[\nat br, nat bc, nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Matrix[\RR64,br,bc\], p: ZZ32, nh: ZZ32, k: ZZ32, _: N[\a\], _: N[\b\], _: N[\c\]): Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\] =
92	    HeadsView[\br,bc,a,b,c\](base, p, nh, k)
93	heads[\nat br, nat bc\](base: Matrix[\RR64,br,bc\], p: ZZ32, nh: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
94	    (nr, nc) = base.sizes
95	    headsN(base, p, nh, k, reflect((nr DIV p) nh), reflect(p), reflect(k))
96	  end
97	object UnheadsView[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat r, nat cc\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], nh: ZZ32)
98	        extends Matrix[\RR64,r,cc\]
99	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c)) end
100	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c), x) end
101	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c), x) end
102	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,r,0,cc\] = array2[\U,r,cc\]()
103	end
104	unheadsN[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat r, nat cc\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], nh: ZZ32, _: N[\r\], _: N[\cc\]): Matrix[\RR64,r,cc\] =
105	    UnheadsView[\a,b,c,r,cc\](base, nh)
106	unheads[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], nh: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
107	    (np, p, k) = t.sizes
108	    unheadsN(t, nh, reflect((np DIV nh) p), reflect(nh k))
109	  end
110	(* a plane of a rank-3 array as a matrix, and every plane transposed *)
111	object PlaneView[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32) extends Matrix[\RR64,b,c\]
112	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get((p, i, j)) end
113	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put((p, i, j), x) end
114	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0((p, i, j), x) end
115	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,b,0,c\] = array2[\U,b,c\]()
116	end
117	plane[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = PlaneView[\a,b,c\](t, p)
118	object Transposed3[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]) extends Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\]
119	    get(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.get((p, j, i)) end
120	    put(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.put((p, j, i), x) end
121	    init0(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.init0((p, j, i), x) end
122	    replica[\U\](): Array3[\U,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = array3[\U,a,c,b\]()
123	end
124	
125	(* ------------------------------------------------- rank-3 algebra -------- *)
126	(* +.×⍤2 : the library product on every pair of planes *)
127	opr juxtaposition[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat a2, nat b2, nat c2\](x: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], y: Array3[\RR64,0,a2,0,b2,0,c2\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
128	    (np, n, d) = x.sizes
129	    (yp, yn, yd) = y.sizes
130	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, yd)
131	    for p <- 0#np do (plane(out, p)).assign((plane(x, p)) (plane(y, p))) end
132	    out
133	  end
134	(* m +⍤2 t : a matrix added to every plane *)
135	opr +[\nat r, nat c, nat a, nat b, nat d\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,d\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
136	    t.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), e: RR64): RR64 => do (p, i, j) = ix; m[i,j] + e end)
137	
138	(* -------------------------------------------------- the row lift --------- *)
139	(* f⍤1 : f on every row of m, the results stacked; the dyadic form pairs the
140	   rows of two matrices; over a rank-3 array the rows are those of every plane.
141	   A parallel for over the rows, each written through a row view. *)
142	rows[\nat r, nat c\](f: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
143	    (n, d) = m.sizes
144	    out = array[\RR64\](n, d)
145	    for i <- 0#n do (row(out, i)).assign(f(row(m, i))) end
146	    out
147	  end
148	rows[\nat r, nat c, nat r2, nat c2\](f: (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], y: Matrix[\RR64,r2,c2\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
149	    (n, d) = x.sizes
150	    out = array[\RR64\](n, d)
151	    for i <- 0#n do (row(out, i)).assign(f(row(x, i), row(y, i))) end
152	    out
153	  end
154	rows[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](f: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
155	    (np, n, d) = t.sizes
156	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, d)
157	    for p <- 0#np, i <- 0#n do (row3(out, p, i)).assign(f(row3(t, p, i))) end
158	    out
159	  end
160	rows[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat a2, nat b2, nat c2\](f: (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], y: Array3[\RR64,0,a2,0,b2,0,c2\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
161	    (np, n, d) = x.sizes
162	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, d)
163	    for p <- 0#np, i <- 0#n do (row3(out, p, i)).assign(f(row3(x, p, i), row3(y, p, i))) end
164	    out
165	  end
166	
167	(* ----------------------------------------------------------- keys -------- *)
168	(* the rows of m at the keys: m[ks;]; the elements of v at the keys: v[ks] *)
169	gather[\T extends Number, nat r, nat c, nat k\](m: Matrix[\T,r,c\], ks: Vector[\ZZ32,k\]): Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
170	    (nr, nc) = m.sizes
171	    array[\T\](|ks|, nc).tabulate(fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): T => m[ks[i], j])
172	  end

## 1. The blocks, on each path

### 1.1 Walk: tasks and the pool (`interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`)

- **The pool.** `FortressTaskRunnerGroup` is a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool` (`FortressTaskRunnerGroup.java:16-33`, asyncMode false, so LIFO local queues). `FortressTaskRunner` is its worker thread. It holds a `volatile BaseTask task`, the "current task" through which every transaction is found (`FortressTaskRunner.java:27`, `:54-61`).
- **Tasks.** `BaseTask extends RecursiveAction` (`BaseTask.java:21`). A child copies its parent's transaction when it is constructed (`:35`). So **the implicit threads of an `atomic` block share the block's transaction object**.
- **`TupleTask`.** It is the unit for tuples, call arguments and `do … also` arms. `compute()` makes itself the current task, catches every `Exception` into `err` and nulls its transaction (`TupleTask.java:33-52`). `Evaluator.forDo` and `evalExprListParallel` save the current task, call `ForkJoinTask.invokeAll`, restore the current task, and only then rethrow the first recorded exception (`Evaluator.java:239-283`, `:336-362`). So **a group always waits for every arm, also when one arm throws or aborts**. That is the specification's fork-join rule (§4).
- **Throttle.** Arguments and tuples fork only while `getSurplusQueuedTaskCount() <= 3` (`TupleTask.java:119-121`, `Evaluator.java:342`). `forDo` has no such check.
- **`spawn`.** Each `spawn` makes a new one-thread pool (`interpreter/glue/prim/Thread.java:55-56`). `val()` and `wait()` busy-spin on a volatile flag (`SpawnTask.java:56-68`). A spawned task has no parent transaction (`SpawnTask` calls `super()`), so a `spawn` inside `atomic` runs outside the transaction. The specification forbids `spawn` inside `atomic` (`spawn.tex:28-31`), and nothing checks it. Row 938 is the spinning on an abrupt end.

### 1.2 Walk: the STM (`interpreter/evaluator/transactions/`, `interpreter/env/ReferenceCell.java`, `ValueNode.java`)

**Shape.** It descends from DSTM. Every mutable variable, mutable field and array element is a `ReferenceCell`. `AtomicArray` is one cell per element (`AtomicArray.java:26-37`). A cell holds a chain of `ValueNode`s, each with a value, a writer transaction, a set of readers and the older node (`ValueNode.java:23-34`). A transaction is a status in an `AtomicReference`: ACTIVE, COMMITTED, ABORTED or ORPHANED (`Transaction.java:36-46`).

- **Commit** is one compare-and-set from ACTIVE to COMMITTED (`Transaction.java:229-260`). A cell's `cleanup()` then reads a committed writer's node as the value, or as the value of the parent transaction for a nested commit. It pops an aborted writer's node (`ReferenceCell.java:87-121`). This is DSTM's "locator" scheme: the value is decided by the owner's status.
- **Readers are visible, and conflicts are detected eagerly.**
  - A transactional read registers the transaction in the node's read set, a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` (`ValueNode.java:66-72`, `ReadSet.java:68-84`).
  - A transactional write first resolves conflicts with every active reader that is not an ancestor, and with the writer (`ValueNode.java:95-116`). It then pushes a new node (`ReferenceCell.java:151-153`).
  - So validation at commit is only a status check (`BaseTask.java:91-100`).
- **Strong atomicity.** Plain access outside `atomic` is isolated from transactions. A non-transactional read aborts any active writer of the cell (`ReferenceCell.java:166-171`). A non-transactional write aborts every reader and writer (`:134-140`). The team added this in "Fixes for atomic/non-atomic interactions" (1d6d275bb, chf, 2008-02-13).
- **Nesting.** Nesting is closed. A nested `atomic` creates `new Transaction(parent)` (`tasks/BaseTask.java:105-121`), and an abort orphans its children (`Transaction.java:267-307`).
- **Contention manager and retries.** `GreedyManager` is wired in (`FortressTaskRunner.java:26`). Despite its name, it **always aborts the other transaction** (`GreedyManager.java:32-49`). Retries are unbounded and have no backoff (`FortressTaskRunner.java:147-175`).
- **`tryatomic`** runs the body once (`Evaluator.java:205-232`). Inside a transaction it is flattened into plain code (`:211-214`), which is defect N6 (§7).
- **Cost outside `atomic`.** Every cell access takes the cell's monitor and consults the transaction, and a write allocates a node, a `ReadSet` and a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` (`c4-parallelism.md` §6). The measured share was 0.8 % of allocation samples in a four-thread C4 run, not the bottleneck (`c4-parallelism.md`, "Measured, 2026-09-19").

### 1.3 Compiled: tasks and the pool (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`, `FortressTaskRunner*`, `FortressExecutable.java`)

- **Pool and tasks.** The pool is again a `ForkJoinPool` (`FortressTaskRunnerGroup.java:33`), sized by `FORTRESS_THREADS`, or half the CPUs when unset (`FortressExecutable.java:37-45`). A generated task class per arm extends `BaseTask`, whose constructor copies the parent's transaction (`BaseTask.java:83-86`).
- **Forking.** `forkIfProfitable` forks while the surplus queue is at most `spawnThreshold`, 5 by default (`:113-144`). `joinOrRun` runs an unforked task inline, and joins a forked one with the current task saved and restored (`:146-178`).
- **Arms.** `genParallelExprs` forks arms n-1 down to 1, runs arm 0 in place, then joins left to right (`CodeGen.java:1635-1712`). It does so only on the normal path: there is no handler that joins the remaining arms when one throws. That is defect N1.
- **Tuples and operators** fork only where `ParallelismAnalyzer` marked the node "worthy" (`CodeGen.java:5233-5236`).
- **Call arguments are evaluated in order** (`CodeGen.evalArg`, `:6935-6955`, under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???" at `:6939`). That is defect N5.

### 1.4 Compiled: the STM (`runtimeSystem/Transaction.java`)

**Shape.** This is a different algorithm: one global sequence lock, buffered writes and value-based validation. In form it is NOrec (Dalessandro, Spear and Scott, PPoPP 2010), though the code cites no paper.

- **The lock.** `global_lock` is an `AtomicInteger`; an odd value means a commit is writing back (`Transaction.java:76`, `:120-158`). Each transaction keeps a `snapshot` of it.
- **Reads.** A read takes the committed value. While the snapshot differs from the lock, it revalidates every recorded read by value and reads again. It then returns an own or ancestral write if there is one, and records the read (`:212-231`).
- **Writes** go to a private `Hashtable` (`:287-297`).
- **Commit.**
  - A read-only transaction returns at once (`:301`).
  - Otherwise the commit takes the lock by compare-and-set from its snapshot, revalidating whenever that fails (`:306-310`).
  - A top-level commit writes back, and a nested commit merges its reads and writes into its parent (`:312-344`, with the team's "This is subtle" comment at `:328`).
  - It releases the lock to the next even value (`:346`).
- **Conflict policy.** The committer wins; there is no contention manager. The generated handler retries without bound and calls `delayTransaction` (`CodeGen.java:1774-1802`). That backs off only when `FORTRESS_EXP_BACKOFF` is set; its default is off, "no evidence that it helps" (`FortressExecutable.java:33`, `BaseTask.java:214-230`).
- **Non-transactional access** is a plain volatile read or write of the cell (`MutableFValue.java:18-29`). Generated code chooses between the two at every access by calling `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`VarCodeGen.java:326-362`, `:483-546`; row 641). So **atomicity is weak**: plain accesses neither take nor check the lock (defect N2).
- `TransactionRecord.java` is an unused placeholder: `TXAbort` throws "Placeholder for now" (`:34-36`).

### 1.5 Compiled: arrays inside transactions (`compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java`, batch 28)

- **The `Object[]` store.** Inside a transaction, `get` and `put` go to `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`, keyed by the array and the index (`FortressArrayStore.java:45-57`, `Transaction.java:31-62`). Outside one, they are `VarHandle` volatile accesses. `init` is a compare-and-set from null outside a transaction, and a transactional read-then-write inside one (`:60-66`).
- **The `double[]` store** (`FortressRR64ArrayStore.java`) "takes no part in a transaction" (its header comment).
- **The prelude's `ZZ32Vector`** is a plain `int[]` with no transaction check (`FZZ32Vector.java:18`, `simpleIntVector.java:26-29`). That is defect N8.

### 1.6 The code generator's `atomic`

`forAtomicBlock` registers its exception-table entry before it emits the body (`CodeGen.java:1783`), so an outer block's handler precedes an inner one's (rows 934, 937; row 888 is the same for `try`). Its other gaps:

- It catches only `TransactionAbortException` (`:1780`), so a Fortress exception leaves the transaction pushed (row 324).
- It has no case for `AtomicExpr` or `TryAtomicExpr` (rows 875, 353).
- Mutable fields bypass the transaction (`VarCodeGen.java:209`, `:220`; row 319).

### 1.7 `ParallelismAnalyzer`

It is a syntactic heuristic: a node is worthy when at least `ARG_THRESHOLD = 2` of its operands are "compute intensive" (`ParallelismAnalyzer.java:44`, `:113-118`). Its defects:

- Every named function is added as compute intensive (`:218`), but the removal targets the `FnDecl` node, not the name (`:225`). So every named call counts.
- Calls whose text contains `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` or `println` are skipped (`:199-203`, with the team's comment "Is this right? The builtins could be intensive too, no?" at `:194`).
- "TODO: I don't think this handles mutual recursion" (`:40`).

### 1.8 Library: ranges, generators, reductions, `parloop`

- **The one library's parallel range.** `loop` splits at a power-of-two boundary into `do … also do … end`, down to single elements, with no grain size. `generate` joins the halves as a call's arguments, `red.join(loop'(lo,mid-1), loop'(mid,hi))` (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1308-1342`, `:1320`). The split depends only on `(lo, hi)`, so the join tree is deterministic (`c4-parallelism.md` §4).
- **`GeneratorLibrary.fss`** only composes generators; it has no `also` of its own.
- **Reductions** carry their algebra as objects: `join` and `empty`, with associativity assumed and checked nowhere (`FortressLibrary.fss:3412`; `c4-parallelism.md` §4).
- **`Matrix.mul`** splits rows and columns with `also` and runs the contraction axis in sequence, with the team's comment "If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition" (`FortressLibrary.fss:3046`). A second comment says the cache-oblivious product was dropped "due to lack of support for atomic increment of matrix elements" (`:3175-3177`). That text dates to 2008 at least (moved by jmaessen's library reorganization 1d2680d4d, 2008-03-24).
- **The compiler prelude.** `parloop` halves at the midpoint while the chunk is above `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK`, default 1 (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:357-369`). `gen` passes its halves as call arguments, and `seqgen` binds them as statements (`:381-414`). On the compiled path the two run alike (N5).

**Contention and abort policy, side by side**

| | walk | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| detection | eager: at the conflicting read or write, through visible readers | lazy: at validation, by value, when the global lock has moved |
| who wins | `GreedyManager`: always aborts the other | the first to commit |
| retry | `doIt`, unbounded, no backoff | generated handler, unbounded; backoff off by default |
| plain access beside `atomic` | aborts the conflicting transaction (strong) | not isolated (weak, N2) |
| nesting | closed; abort orphans the children | closed; a nested commit merges into the parent under the global lock |
| threads inside a block | share the block's transaction | share the block's transaction (unsafely, N3) |

## 2. Provenance

**Walk's STM began as Sun Labs' DSTM2 and became the team's own.**
- Christine Flood (`chf`) imported DSTM2 into the tree on 2007-06-13: "More Transactional Memory support. DSTM2 is now included in our source tree" (9aed945d8, 56 `dstm2/` paths). `ProjectFortress/src/dstm2/Transaction.java` there carries "Copyright 2006 Sun Microsystems" (`git show 9aed945d8:ProjectFortress/src/dstm2/Transaction.java`).
- Her later commits:
  - "Removed use of DSTM2 Adapters" (cdaf5a5f4, 2007-07-24);
  - "Concurrent Read sets, parallelism inside transactions, transaction tests, a new contention manager, new atomic arrays with single element transaction granularity" (c0331e339, 2007-09-06);
  - "Nested Transactions" (24f2532a7, 2007-10-24);
  - "nested parallel transactions" (37a30e8a1, 2008-07-22), which introduced `ValueNode`;
  - "Don't let orphaned transactions return values, … dial back parallelism" (432d03fe3, 2008-09-05).
- `dstm2/` is absent at a874948ac (`git ls-tree`).
- The contention managers keep DSTM2's `@author` tags: Maurice Herlihy (`AggressiveManager.java:19`, `BackoffManager.java:22`, `Recoverable.java:17`), Bill Scherer (`KarmaManager.java:37`, `KindergartenManager.java:22`, `EruptionManager.java:42`), and `mph` (`AtomicArray.java:20`, `BaseManager.java:20`). These are Scherer and Scott's managers of PODC 2005.
- `FortressManager2` to `5` are the team's own, unguarded debug experiments with priority by transaction number (e.g. `FortressManager5.java`, "We prefer the lowest numbered transaction unless we've retried too often, then we get mad (greedy)").

**The team knowingly gave up Greedy's waiting because of work stealing.**
- DSTM2's original `GreedyManager` is Guerraoui, Herlihy and Pochon's Greedy (PODC 2005), cited in its header: "If prior transaction is waiting or lower priority, then abort it. otherwise, wait for it to commit, abort, or wait" (`git show 9aed945d8:ProjectFortress/src/dstm2/manager/GreedyManager.java`).
- The Fortress `GreedyManager` is "Based on Backoff Manager" (`GreedyManager.java:12`) and never waits. It says why: "There is an interesting interaction between work stealing and transactions. Until we can figure out a way to boost the priority of the transaction keeping everyone else waiting at a join point, this will have to do." (`:22-24`, added in 432d03fe3, chf, 2008-09-05).

**The compiled STM is Flood's of 2012, young when the project stopped.**

content.content:
## 4. Design: what the specification defines, and what each path does

| question | specification | walk | compiled |
|---|---|---|---|
| parallelism inside `atomic` | Implicit threads "will complete before the atomic expression itself does … will see one another's writes; they may synchronize with one another using nested atomic expressions" (`atomic.tex:77-81`). A nested block is atomic with respect to its siblings (`:72-75`; `memory-model.tex:416`). | children share the transaction; nested atomics synchronize them (400); tryatomic does not (N6) | the same sharing; a nested commit merges into the parent; the shared sets are unsafe (N3); nested validation is partial (N4) |
| a task that blocks or joins inside a transaction | A group's thread is suspended until the group completes; `abort` may suspend (`parallelism.tex:149-157`, `transactions.tex:41-45`). `spawn` "cannot be run within the body of an atomic expression" (`spawn.tex:28-31`). | joins are ordinary; a busy wait progresses by aborts; `spawn` runs unchecked outside the transaction | joins are ordinary; a busy wait progresses at revalidation; `spawn` is not compiled (row 82) |
| abort during a fork | `abort` "abandons execution of the innermost atomic expression" (`transactions.tex:16`). A group "completes abruptly" only after each thread has completed, not run, or ended early (`parallelism.tex:95-99`). | every arm is joined before the retry (PASS) | the retry happens with the other arms unjoined (N1); the innermost block is missed in one body (rows 934, 937) |
| work stealing across transactions | silent | tasks carry their transaction; the current task is restored after `invokeAll`; the manager never waits, so a transaction buried under a helping join is never waited on (`GreedyManager.java:22-24`) | the current task is saved and restored around `join` (revival); there is no waiting except on the sequence lock during write-back |
| plain access beside `atomic` | atomic "with respect to any action performed by any thread which is dynamically outside" (`atomic.tex:36-41`), explicitly including reads and writes outside atomic (`:100-106`); the memory model's predecessor and successor rule (`memory-model.tex:391-400`) | strong | weak (N2) |
| exceptions | variables revert (`atomic.tex:59-70`) | revert (g = 100) | kept (row 324) |
| gather | "Where feasible, reduction must be used in favor of updating a single shared object" (`memory-model.tex:90`); reduction variables in OpenMP style (`reduction.tex:67-79`), "not yet supported" (`:15`) | reductions are parallel and exact (row 60) | reductions run in sequence (N5) |

**The design is coherent: fork/join and STM fit together in it.** Its implicit threads inside a block are *closed nesting with parallel children*. Research systems built exactly that a few years later; each found it hard, and each answered with an ancestor-aware validation:

- Agrawal, Fineman and Sukha, "Nested parallelism in transactional memory", PPoPP 2008 ([researchr](https://researchr.org/publication/AgrawalFS08));
- Volos et al., "NePaLTM", ECOOP 2009, which calls itself the first TM to support nested parallelism inside transactions ([bibtex](https://bibtex.github.io/ECOOP-2009-VolosWASTN.html));
- Barreto et al., "Leveraging parallel nesting in transactional memory", PPoPP 2010, which names "efficiently answering the ancestor test" as the core difficulty ([Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/?p=163756)).

Production STMs, by my knowledge and not checked online here, avoided the problem altogether: Haskell's `atomically` admits no I/O or `forkIO`, and its types confine `TVar`s, which gives strong atomicity for free; Clojure's `dosync` runs nothing in parallel and holds agent sends until commit. The memory model itself compares a condition with "the X10 guys" (`memory-model.tex:440`); X10's `atomic`, by my knowledge, may not spawn activities.

Strong atomicity in an STM costs barriers on plain accesses. Shpeisman et al., PLDI 2007, built it with barriers, made cheaper by an analysis that spots data still private to one thread ([typeset](https://typeset.io/papers/enforcing-isolation-and-ordering-in-stm-8nbb5fqzpp)). Fortress's specification plans the same economy with shared and local objects, so that atomic access to a local object is cheap (`shared-local.tex:12-60`), but "the present Fortress implementation immediately makes every object shared" (`:40`).

The design's real weaknesses are three:
1. Two commitments that are expensive to deliver: strong atomicity and parallel nesting.
2. A programming discipline that nothing checks. The memory model's principles ask that "it must be possible to check that a program obeys the programming discipline" (`memory-model.tex:49-50`); no checker exists, and races are silent (row 59).
3. Its own gather tool, reduction variables, was never built.

## 5. The JVM side, in Goetz's and the JMM's terms

**Walk.**
- *Locking.* All of a cell's state is guarded by the cell's intrinsic lock (`ReferenceCell.java:87`, `:123`, `:163`), so its accesses are totally ordered: Goetz's "guarded by" rule. The cost is a monitor per element.
- *Atomic variables.* A transaction's status is an `AtomicReference` changed by compare-and-set, so commit and abort are linearizable (`Transaction.java:229-307`).
- *Publication.* Transactions reach other threads through monitor-guarded nodes or through `fork`; both are safe publication.
- *Busy waiting.* `SpawnTask` spins without `Thread.onSpinWait` and without `ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker` (`:56-68`), a liveness hazard.
- *Iteration.* `CopyOnWriteArrayList` read sets are safe to iterate, at O(n) per add.

**Compiled.**
- *The sequence lock* is a correct NOrec in JMM terms. Values and the lock are both volatile, so "read the value, then check the lock" is ordered in the synchronization order. Write-back is bracketed by compare-and-set on the lock (`Transaction.java:212-231`, `:299-347`).
- *Defects against Goetz.* What departs from Goetz is thread confinement assumed where there is none:
  - A `Transaction` is shared by sibling tasks (`BaseTask.java:86`), but its `Hashtable` is iterated without the table's lock, which `Hashtable` requires for compound iteration (N3).
  - `snapshot.set(TXValidate())` is a check-then-act race between siblings, benign but unprincipled (`:216-217`).
  - Two shared mutable counters are updated without synchronization: `allRetries` and `totalElapsedTime` (`FortressTaskRunnerGroup.java:37-41`).
  - `FException` keeps every exception value in a static, unsynchronized, never-read `HashMap` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FException.java:18`, `:26`). That is a data race on a shared map and a leak. It was found by reading only, not reproduced.
- *Fork and join publication.*
  - The class comment declines to fork in a constructor because of final-field semantics, "a memory model disaster" (`BaseTask.java:29-37`), a sound reading.
  - A task's fields are published by `fork()`'s release and read back after `join()`. `ForkJoinTask` implements `Future`, whose memory-consistency guarantee makes actions in the task happen before the joiner's next action.
  - Disjoint element writes by tasks are race-free: the JLS has no word tearing between distinct array elements (17.6), and `join` orders them before the reader. This is the ground microGPT's data-parallel writes stand on.
  - N1 breaks it: an orphaned arm's writes have no happens-before edge to the code that follows the group.
- *Volatile is stronger than the language needs.* Every plain access to a cell, and to an element of the `Object[]` store, is volatile (`MutableFValue.java:18`; `FortressArrayStore.java:47`, `:55`). The specification asks only indivisibility (`memory-model.tex:252-260`) and program order for accesses that "certainly access the same location" (`:285-286`). `VarHandle` opaque mode gives exactly that, bitwise atomic for `double` too and without fences; plain mode may tear a `double` (JLS 17.7). This matters for P-84's `double[]` store.
- *The revival's changes.* The move from `jsr166y` to `java.util.concurrent` changed three behaviours:
  - j.u.c's `join` helps by running other queued tasks. That broke the "current task" invariant, and the fix in `joinOrRun` saves and restores it (`BaseTask.java:150-177`). The fix is right for the forked branch. The unforked branch runs `compute()` inline and leaves the child as the current task (row 876). That drift stays consistent only while transactions nest along one thread, which holds today and should be made explicit by restoring there too.
  - j.u.c re-creates a rethrown exception in the joiner when it has a `(Throwable)` or no-argument constructor (the `DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.newInstance` frames in N3's trace). `FException` has neither, so Fortress exceptions keep their identity.
  - Compensation threads can lift the pool above `FORTRESS_THREADS` (`size = 5`, §3.3).

## 6. microGPT

**Under walk today.**
- Neither program writes `atomic`, `spawn` or `also` (`grep` over `explorations/run-c4/src/*.fss` and `explorations/apl/mg/*.fss`: no match). Their writes are private, disjoint fills, or sequential (`c4-parallelism/audit.md` §4).
- They reach the pool through parallel `for`, tuples, arguments, and the library's `fill`, `map` and `mul`; reductions through `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX`; and every array element as a `ReferenceCell` with no transaction open (`c4-parallelism.md` §§2-6).
- The gather is reductions and products, including the embedding gradients, written as one-hot products (`MicroGptFlat.fss:70`; APL `MicroGptApl.fss:96`). **No transaction is ever opened.**

**On the compiled path, with unboxed arrays and views** (P-17, P-84, F-11, F-12, F-40, F-301):
- **The pool and `do … also`.** Loops over views fork per arm. This is sound with disjoint writes (§5), but the one library splits to single elements with no grain size (`RangeInternals.fss:1324-1340`). Each split builds a task object even when it is not forked (`CodeGen.java:1667-1689`).
- **Reductions.** They will run in sequence (N5). Every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of the model loses its parallelism unless the code generator or the library changes.
- **Abrupt completion.** Any exception in a forked arm, such as `IntegerOverflow`, an index fault in a view, or an `assert`, leaves sibling arms writing arrays after the caller has moved on (N1).
- **The per-access transaction check.** It stays on mutable locals (row 641, F-12). For elements, the `Object[]` store checks the thread and the current transaction on every `get` and `put` (`FortressArrayStore.java:35-37`). Whether the unboxed store pays the same is undecided (§8, D1).
- **The STM** is not reached, if the model keeps its shape.

**The gather can be done by reductions alone, as the language intends.** Only a scatter-add, such as an embedding gradient indexed by token, would tempt `atomic`. Both programs avoid it with one-hot products. The library's own authors also chose sequence over atomic increments (`FortressLibrary.fss:3046`, `:3175-3177`). Parallelising the contraction axis needs a reduction, private partial results joined, not `atomic`. Given the cost in §3.3, an atomic gather would be slower than a sequential one.

content.content:
## 2. What the team's sources require

### 2.1 The specification

- **Every location the block touches belongs to it.** "All reads and all writes which occur as part of this evaluation will appear to occur simultaneously in a single atomic step with respect to any action performed by any thread which is dynamically outside" (`atomic.tex:37-41`). "Dynamically" means by what runs, not where the code is written, so a function called from a block is inside it.
- **Mutable variables are locations.** "Allocation occurs when a mutable variable is declared, or when a reference object is constructed" (`basic/evaluation/memory-ops.tex:36-39`). The team wasn't sure: "Should variables (esp parameters and mutable locals) be considered locations ...?" (`basic/memory-model.tex:360-363`).
- **Strong atomicity.** A block is atomic also against accesses outside every block: "with respect to reads and writes of a_i and sum that do not occur in atomic expressions" (`atomic.tex:104-106`). *Weak atomicity* protects a block only against other blocks.
- **The discipline.** A program that keeps it needs no strong atomicity: "Updates to shared mutable locations must always be performed using an atomic expression. A location is considered to be shared if and only if that location can be accessed by more than one thread at a time" (`memory-model.tex:69-75`).
- **What a block must undo.** On an exception, "all writes to objects allocated before the atomic expression began evaluation are discarded. Writes to newly allocated objects are retained. Any variable reverts to the value it held before evaluation of the atomic expression began" (`atomic.tex:63-67`). `abort()` "rolls back its changes, requiring the atomic expression to execute again from the beginning" (`advanced/parallelism-locality/transactions.tex:15-19`).
- **Nesting.** An inner block is atomic against the other threads of its outer block (`atomic.tex:72-81`).
- **Shared and local objects.** "A local object must be transitively reachable ... from the variables of at most one running thread. A local object may be accessed more cheaply than a shared object, particularly in the case of atomic reads and writes" (`advanced/parallelism-locality/shared-local.tex:19-23`). A local variable that a thread reads must be *published*, made shared, before that thread runs in parallel (`:47-50`). The team never built this: "the present Fortress implementation immediately makes every object shared" (`:40`).
- **Modifiers.** An `io` function "must not be invoked from a non-`io` function", and `io` functions "cannot be called within an atomic expression"; a function marked `atomic` runs its body as a block (`basic/functions.tex:118-126`; `atomic.tex:50-57`). Both are "not yet supported" (`atomic.tex:15`).

### 2.2 The team's later word

- The 2012 restart has a header for atomic expressions and nothing under it (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/atomic.tick:12`). Its `do … also` text keeps the `atomic` modifier of each block (`do-also.tick:18-37`).
- The papers under `Papers/` say nothing on transactions or `atomic` (grep, no match outside bibliographies).

### 2.3 The team's two implementations

- **Walk.** Every mutable variable, field and array element is a cell that takes its own lock and consults the transaction at every access, inside `atomic` or not. A plain access aborts a conflicting transaction, so walk is strongly atomic (parallelism review, section 1.2).
- **The compiled path.** The code generator, not the run time, writes the check, at every read and write of four kinds of variable (`compiler/codegen/VarCodeGen.java`):
  - `LocalMutableVar`, a `var` local in its own method's frame (`:454-560`; the cell is made at `:466-474`; the checks at `:484-513` and `:523-551`);
  - `MutableTaskVarCodeGen`, a `var` local captured by a task arm, a function expression or a local function, which reaches the cell through a field (`:612-745`; made for every capture at `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:5441-5462`, for task arms through `delegate`, `:5581-5611`, for function expressions at `:3924-3945` and for local functions at `:4079-4107`);
  - `MutableStaticBinding`, a top-level `var` (`VarCodeGen.java:313-414`);
  - `MutableFieldVar`, an object's `var` field, whose cell the object holds (`:207-239`).
- An immutable field has no check (`FieldVar`, `:174-199`).
- **The array store** checks too, in Java, in every `get` and `put` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java:35-57`). This is the element side of the same question.
- **The compiled STM** is in the form of NOrec: one global sequence lock, buffered writes, validation by value (`runtimeSystem/Transaction.java:83`, `:228-248`, `:302-371`; parallelism review, section 1.4). A plain access neither takes nor checks the lock, so the compiled path is weakly atomic (gap-ledger row 948).
- **What the check reads.** The current thread, a cast, a non-final boxed static `Boolean debug` (`BaseTask.java:50`), the thread's `volatile` task field twice (`runtimeSystem/FortressTaskRunner.java:19`), and the task's transaction (`BaseTask.java:255-263`).

### 2.4 Who wrote it, and whether they planned to remove it

- Christine Flood wrote the compiled transactions; her bio names "software transactional memory, and compilation to a fork/join framework" (`research/authorship.md:46`). The checks first appear in her "Top Level Transactions" (9f63f9859, 2012-04-09), four sites in `VarCodeGen.java` calling `FortressAction.inATransaction`; the snapshot of 2012-03-20 (5e6f71081f) has none (`git show REV:…/VarCodeGen.java | grep -c inATransaction`: 4 and 0). Nested transactions followed in May 2012 (11beddd1d, d3f49be2f, 8415fc990), and Claire Alvis's backoff on 2012-06-04 (parallelism review, section 2). 9f63f9859 and 11beddd1d have no parent in the conversion, so an earlier change can be hidden (`research/authorship.md`, caveats).
- The revival added the top-level `var` (42d51c474, 2026-09-19) and the `var` field in a cell (F-374, the FACTS entry on the field's cell), each with the same check.
- **No plan to remove the checks is left.** I found no comment, stub or note on their cost in `VarCodeGen.java`, `CodeGen.java`, `BaseTask.java` or `Transaction.java`. The one stub near them is about tasks: "I'm just a stub. Someday I'll have a body that updates the changed local variables" (`CodeGen.java:5561`).
- **The team's bytecode optimizer** (Flood, Chase and Steele) is a separate jar-to-jar tool that `fortress compile` doesn't run (`compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/ByteCodeOptimizer.java:130-141`, `bin/BytecodeOptimize`). None of its passes treats the checks.
- The team's one plan for cheaper atomic access is the specification's shared and local objects (2.1).

### 2.5 The record, and where the tree moved since the parallelism review

- FACTS, the record's established facts: F-12 (a scalar loop pays a check at each use of its accumulator), F-351 (a compiled transaction validates itself and every ancestor), F-374 (a `var` field is a cell, and every access pays the check). POSITIONS, the curator's decisions: P-169 (the compiled store is an `Object[]` whose elements the transaction tracks by array and index; F-333). No other decision is on `atomic` or transactions (searched by title and by grep).
- **Moved since the parallelism review** (2026-11-08, at f5aa647de):
  - The transaction's repairs (594da41299; F-351) closed gap-ledger rows 933, 934, 937 and 324, and the review's defects N3 and N4 (rows 949, 950).
  - Climb batch 30's rung P (76b21f4981; F-350; P-175, the decision that a call's arguments fork) joins every forked arm (rows 947, 951), and the one library's parallel range stops at a grain of 16 elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1312-1330`).
  - Row 319 is closed, so a `var` field now pays the check (F-374); the review's section 1.6 predates this.
- **Still open:** row 948, strong atomicity, which is review-queue item 510 (question D2, not yet asked); row 984, the same for a nested block; row 953, unboxed array elements outside the transaction, which is item 509 (question D1, not yet asked).

### 2.6 So: which variables can a transaction reach, by the specification?

This is my reading of 2.1. It isn't stated in one place.

- A block must undo, and must isolate, only locations that **existed before the block began** (`atomic.tex:63-67`). A location allocated inside the innermost open block needs no tracking by it. No thread outside can see it before the commit, and an abort makes it unreachable.
- So a `var` local that no closure captures (one thread's frame alone) is reached by a transaction only at an access written **inside an `atomic` block of its own body, when the declaration is outside that block**. Everywhere else, either no transaction is open, or the local was allocated inside the open one.
- A local captured only by a task arm keeps that rule. The arm is joined before its group ends (F-350), so it runs under the transactions open where it was written.
- A local captured by a function expression or a local function, a top-level `var`, a `var` field and an array element can be reached by any transaction that calls the code. That can be decided only by what runs, or by a whole-program analysis.

How each answer to D2 changes this:

- **D2(a), weak atomicity kept.** A check can go wherever the code is shown to run in no transaction, and tracking can go for a location allocated after the innermost open block began.
- **D2(b), plain writes take the sequence lock.** A plain write to any location that some transaction may read must pay a compare-and-set pair. For a plain read to be atomic too, it must wait while a commit writes back (inferred). Only a location that one thread alone reaches, or that no transaction ever touches, skips.
- **D2(c), shared and local objects.** Only shared objects pay the barrier. An uncaptured local is always local. A captured cell becomes shared when its task runs in parallel (`shared-local.tex:47-50`).

References: the lines above (specification files under `Specification/`, Java under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`); `explorations/reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1, 2, 4, D1 and D2; `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, items 509, 510; FACTS and POSITIONS as named.

extends Array1[\T,b1,s1\]
    get(i:ZZ32): T = mem.get(0,i)
    put(i:ZZ32,v:T): () = mem.put((0,i),v)
    init0(i:ZZ32,v:T): () = mem.init0((0,i),v)
    offset(i:ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (_,r) = mem.offset(0,i); r end
    toIndex(i:ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (_,r) = mem.toIndex(0,i); r end
    subarray[\nat b, nat s, nat o\](m: ZZ32): Array1[\T, b, s\] =
        Row[\T,b,s\](mem.subarray[\0,1,b,s,0,o\](1,m))
end

trait AnyMatrix end

trait Matrix[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat s0, nat s1\]
        extends { AnyMatrix, Array2[\T, 0, s0, 0, s1\], AdditiveGroup[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\] }
        excludes { AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    fill(v:T):Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = do
        for i <- zeroIndices() do init0(i,v) end
        self
      end
    tabulate(f:(ZZ32,ZZ32)->T):Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = do
        for i <- zeroIndices() do init0(i,f(toIndex(i))) end
        self
      end
    opr +(self, v:Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] =
        cast[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\](ivmap[\T\](fn (i:(ZZ32,ZZ32),e:T):T => e + v.get(i)))
    opr -(self, v:Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] =
        cast[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\](ivmap[\T\](fn (i:(ZZ32,ZZ32),e:T):T => e - v.get(i)))
    opr -(self): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = cast[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\](map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => - e))
    scale(t1: T): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = cast[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\](map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => t1 e))
    mul[\ nat s2 \](other: Matrix[\T,s1,s2\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s2\] = do
        res = matrix[\T,s0,s2\]()
        mma(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                pr : T = get(a,b) other.get(b,c)
                (* If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition. *)
                res.put((a,c), res.get(a,c) + pr)
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                do
                  mma(a,i,b,j,c,k0)
                also do
                  mma(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1)
                end
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mma(a,i,b,j0,c,k)

            else

                do

                end
            end
        mm(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                res.put((a,c), get(a,b) other.get(b,c))
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                do
                  mm(a,i,b,j,c,k0)
                also do

            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mm(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                do
                  mm(a,i0,b,j,c,k)
                also do
                  mm(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k)

            SUM[\T\][(j,v_j)<-v.indexValuePairs] v_j get(j,i)

content.content:
## 5. Vectorisation: what HotSpot did with the baseline's loops

**How this is known.** `hsdis` is not on this machine (`Loading hsdis library failed`). Without it, `-XX:CompileCommand=print` prints a compiled method's machine code as hex; `asm-count.py` cuts it per method, disassembles it with `objdump` and counts the double-precision arithmetic instructions by kind. `./run.sh asm` compiles each method alone (`dontinline`) so that the counts can be attributed. Beside it: the same timings with `-XX:-UseSuperWord`, and the Vector API variant. The debug build's traces are not in this product JDK: `-XX:+PrintOptoAssembly` is accepted and prints no listing.

    FlatArrays::mul       1288 bytes | packed double arithmetic: none       | scalar: 12
    FlatArrays::tMul      1592 bytes | packed double arithmetic: none       | scalar: 12
    FlatArrays::mulT      1072 bytes | packed double arithmetic: 2 on ymm   | scalar: 12
    FlatArrays::addMulT   1112 bytes | packed double arithmetic: 2 on ymm   | scalar: 13
    FlatArrays::dot        648 bytes | packed double arithmetic: 2 on ymm   | scalar: 12
    FlatArrays::sum        352 bytes | packed double arithmetic: none       | scalar:  6
    FlatArrays::addInto    648 bytes | packed double arithmetic: 5 on zmm   | scalar:  2
    FlatArrays::headsMul  1544 bytes | packed double arithmetic: none       | scalar: 12
    MicroGptFlat::rmsn     632 bytes | packed double arithmetic: none       | scalar:  9
    MicroGptFlat$6::run   1296 bytes | packed double arithmetic: 42 on zmm  | scalar: 28      (adam's loop)

No method has a fused multiply-add. By loop shape:

| Loop shape | Where | Vectorised by C2? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `out[ro+j] += s * w[rw+j]`: two rows at different offsets | `mul`, `tMul`, `headsMul`, `headsTMul`: all the backward products | **No.** The two ranges could overlap in one array, and C2 in this JDK neither proves that they do not nor checks it at run time | no packed instruction; the same time with superword off (table below); `./run.sh axpy`: 0.42 to 0.71 ns per element at every length |
| the same loop with one index on two arrays, `o[j] += s * w[j]` (what rows as `double[][]` would give) | not in the baseline | yes, but it pays only for long loops | `./run.sh axpy`: 0.42, 0.19, 0.13 and 0.17 ns per element at lengths 16, 64, 256 and 4,096, against 0.71, 0.44, 0.39 and 0.42 |
| `s += a[i] * b[i]`: a sum of products | `mulT`, `addMulT`, `dot`: the forward products and the norms | **Half.** The products are packed four at a time (ymm); the additions stay one after another, because a `double` sum keeps its order. It does not pay: with superword off most of these loops are faster | 2 packed multiplies, scalar adds; `mulT` 16x16: 1.33 microseconds with, 1.10 without |
| `s += x[i]` | `sum` | no | none packed |
| elementwise, every array at the same index | `adam`'s loop, `addInto` | **Yes**, 8 doubles at a time (zmm), divisions and square roots included | 42 packed instructions; `adam` takes 10.8 microseconds with superword and 20.7 without |
| `out[oo+j] = x[xo+j] / r` and the other row loops of the model | `rmsn`, `rmsn_b`, `sm_b` | no (the offsets differ, as in the first row) | none packed |

So the step's hot loops, the products, run as scalar code: about 0.33 to 0.36 ns per multiply-add in the products of 16 by 16 (0.8 cycles at 2.3 GHz). Only Adam's update is vectorised. What the check's tolerance would allow: a vectorised sum of products changes the order of the additions; the Vector API variant below does that in `mulT` and `addMulT` and still passes every check, with differences no larger than the baseline's.

**Per operation**, each alone at the step's sizes at batch 1, microseconds per call, median of 3 forks' medians (`./run.sh kernels`: 250 ms of warm-up, then 10 samples of 10 ms; load 2.6 at the start and 4.7 at the end, the fork/join configurations of section 6 ran in the same rounds). In the `plain` column the three forks' medians agree within 8 % for every row but four (`mulT` for `pr`: 2.54 to 3.81; `addMulT` for `x2`: 1.27 to 1.66; `tMul` for `gW*`: 1.43 to 2.54; `onehotTMul`: 0.13 to 0.18).

| Operation, shapes, the model's value | plain | superword off | Vector API |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `mulT` 16x16 . (16x16)^T, `q`, `k`, `v` | 1.33 | 1.10 | 0.50 |
| `mulT` 16x16 . (64x16)^T, `m0` | 4.83 | 4.31 | 1.94 |
| `mulT` 16x16 . (27x16)^T, `pr` | 2.56 | 1.85 | 0.87 |
| `addMulT` 16x16 . (16x16)^T, `x2` | 1.40 | 1.13 | 0.56 |
| `addMulT` 16x64 . (16x64)^T, `x4` | 4.65 | 6.08 | 1.60 |
| `mul` 16x16 . 16x16, `dh` and the terms of `dX1` | 1.45 | 1.46 | 0.82 |
| `mul` 16x27 . 27x16, `dX4` | 2.38 | 2.40 | 1.35 |
| `mul` 16x16 . 16x64, `dM0` | 5.08 | 5.17 | 2.27 |
| `mul` 16x64 . 64x16, `dX3` | 5.47 | 5.64 | 2.98 |
| `tMul` (16x16)^T . 16x16, `gWQ`, `gWK`, `gWV`, `gWO` | 1.45 | 1.44 | 0.47 |
| `tMul` (16x27)^T . 16x16, `gLM` | 2.39 | 2.35 | 0.86 |
| `tMul` (16x16)^T . 16x64, `gF2` | 5.05 | 5.05 | 1.82 |
| `tMul` (16x64)^T . 16x16, `gF1` | 5.49 | 5.16 | 1.99 |
| `headsMulTScaleMask`, 4 planes | 1.55 | 1.54 | (plain) |
| `headsMulT`, 4 planes | 1.32 | 1.29 | (plain) |
| `headsMul`, 4 planes | 1.88 | 1.86 | (plain) |
| `headsTMul`, 4 planes | 1.56 | 1.56 | (plain) |
| `rows(sm)`, 64 rows of 16 (1,024 `exp`) | 7.44 | 7.46 | (plain) |
| `rows(sm)`, 16 rows of 27 (432 `exp`) | 3.08 | 3.16 | (plain) |
| `rows(sm_b)`, 64 rows of 16 | 0.63 | 0.64 | (plain) |
| `rows(rmsn)`, 16 rows of 16 | 0.31 | 0.31 | (plain) |
| `rows(rmsn_b)`, 16 rows of 16 | 0.63 | 0.68 | (plain) |
| `onehotTMul` 27x16 | 0.13 | 0.17 | (plain) |
| `adam`, 4,192 elements | 10.77 | 20.69 | (plain) |

Counted over the calls of one step, the products are about 65 % of the measured step and the two softmaxes about 10 %; the times of the operations alone add up to about 80 % of it. The harness's last row, the whole step timed in the same JVM after all the operations, is left out: there the step measured 130 to 152 microseconds, slower than in a JVM that runs only the step, so the step's time is the one of section 4.

**The Vector API variant** (`variants/vector/FlatArrays.java`; `jdk.incubator.vector` is in this JDK as an incubator module, `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector`). It replaces the four products only: `mul` and `tMul` add each element's terms in the baseline's order (a lane per element, no fused multiply-add), `mulT` and `addMulT` split each dot product over the lanes and add the lanes at the end. It passes the 7 and the 40 checks (`./run.sh variants`); its measured differences are 4.4e-16 on both quick losses, 8.3e-17 on the gradient, 5.6e-17 on the parameters after Adam, at most 8.9e-16 on any loss and 5.2e-10 on any finite difference of the full check.

The whole step, by the method of section 4 with 5 forks and the configurations in turn inside each fork (`./run.sh steps`; load 4.5 at the first fork, 2.1 at the last, the fork/join configurations of section 6 in the same rounds), microseconds, median of the fork medians (range), and the smallest sample:

| Configuration | `step1` | min | `train5` | min | `step4` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| plain, the baseline | 101.4 (100.9 to 103.9) | 98.9 | 563.7 (562.2 to 582.0) | 552.9 | 407.1 (404.8 to 413.4) |
| plain, `-XX:-UseSuperWord` | 97.6 (97.6 to 98.7) | 94.7 | 600.8 (596.3 to 603.9) | 582.2 | 414.4 (409.9 to 424.6) |
| Vector API in the four products | 75.5 (70.4 to 76.9) | 68.5 | 431.0 (415.2 to 478.9) | 405.1 | 305.8 (284.0 to 310.5) |

So with superword off the step alone is 4 % faster (the half-vectorised dot products) and the five steps with Adam 7 % slower (Adam's loop). The Vector API in the products alone takes a quarter off the step. The products alone are 1.8 to 3 times faster with it, less than the 8 lanes, because rows of 16 are two vectors long.

### What is not optimal in the baseline

P-7 calls the pure-Java program "the optimal result". This one is the careful scalar program that the brief asked for: `double[]`, plain loops, one thread, the arithmetic of the Fortress. It is not the fastest Java for this model. Measured here: the Vector API in the products gives 75 against 101 microseconds. Not measured: explicit vectors in the other loops, the `exp` of the softmax in vectors, skipping the masked and the padded entries, a batch larger than 1 per step.

## 6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime

(************************************************************
* \subsection*{Reductions}
************************************************************)

trait Reduction[\L\]
    getter reverse():Reduction[\L\]
    abstract empty(): L
    abstract join(a: L, b: L): L
end

(** Invariants:
    join must be associative with identity empty
    unlift(lift(x)) = x
 **)
trait ActualReduction[\R,L\] extends Reduction[\L\]
    abstract empty(): L
    abstract join(a: L, b: L): L
    abstract lift(r:R): L
    abstract unlift(l:L): R
    (** If this reduction left-distributes over r, return a pair of
        reductions with the same lift and unlift **)
    leftDistribute[\K\](r: ActualReduction[\R,K\]): PossibleReductionPair[\K\]
    (** If this reduction right-distributes over r, return a pair of
        reductions with the same lift and unlift **)
    rightDistribute[\K\](r: ActualReduction[\R,K\]): PossibleReductionPair[\K\]
    (** If this reduction distributes over r, return a pair of
        reductions with the same lift and unlift **)
    distribute[\K\](r: ActualReduction[\R,K\]): PossibleReductionPair[\K\]
end

trait PossibleReductionPair[\R\] extends Condition[\PossibleReductionPair[\R\]\]
    comprises { NoReductionPair[\R\], SomeReductionPair[\R\] }
end

object NoReductionPair[\R\] extends PossibleReductionPair[\R\]
    getter holds(): Boolean
    cond[\G\](t:PossibleReductionPair[\R\]->G, e:()->G): G
end

trait SomeReductionPair[\R\] extends PossibleReductionPair[\R\]
    getter holds(): Boolean
    abstract getter outer(): Reduction[\R\]
    abstract getter inner(): Reduction[\R\]
    cond[\G\](t:PossibleReductionPair[\R\]->G, e:()->G): G
end

trait ReductionPair[\R,L\] extends SomeReductionPair[\L\]
    abstract getter outer(): ActualReduction[\R,L\]
    abstract getter inner(): ActualReduction[\R,L\]
end

(** The usual lifting to Maybe for identity-less operators **)
trait AssociativeReduction[\R\] extends ActualReduction[\R,Maybe[\R\]\]
    empty(): Nothing[\R\]
    join(a: Maybe[\R\], b: Maybe[\R\]): Maybe[\R\]
    abstract simpleJoin(a:R, b:R): R
    lift(r:R): Maybe[\R\]
    unlift(r:Maybe[\R\]): R
end

trait SomeCommutativeReduction end (* mark for commutative *)

trait DistributesOver[\E\] end (* marking for distributivity *)

trait CommutativeReduction[\R\] extends {AssociativeReduction[\R\], SomeCommutativeReduction} end

(** Monoids don't require a special lift and unlift operation. **)
trait MonoidReduction[\R\] extends ActualReduction[\R,R\]
    lift(r:R): R
    unlift(r:R): R
end

trait CommutativeMonoidReduction[\R\] extends {MonoidReduction[\R\], SomeCommutativeReduction} end

trait ReductionWithZeroes[\R,L\] extends ActualReduction[\R,L\]
    isLeftZero(l:L): Boolean
    isRightZero(l:L): Boolean
    isZero(l:L): Boolean
end

trait BigOperator[\I,O,R,L\]
    abstract getter reduction(): ActualReduction[\R,L\]
    abstract getter body(): I->R
    abstract getter unwrap(): R->O
end

object BigReduction[\R,L\](reduction:ActualReduction[\R,L\]) extends BigOperator[\R,R,R,L\]
    getter body(): R->R
    getter unwrap(): R->R
end

object Comprehension[\I,O,R,L\](unwrap: R->O, reduction: ActualReduction[\R,L\], body:I->R)
        extends BigOperator[\I,O,R,L\]

object CompactFullParScalarRange(l:ZZ32, r:ZZ32)
        extends { CompactFullScalarRange }
    getter lower(): ZZ32 = l
    getter upper(): ZZ32 = r
    getter left(): Just[\ZZ32\] = Just[\ZZ32\](l)

    seq(self): CompactFullSeqScalarRange = CompactFullSeqScalarRange(l,r)
    generate[\T\](red:Reduction[\T\], body: ZZ32->T): T =
        if r < l then

        else
            loop'(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): T =
                if lo=hi then
                    body(lo)
                elif 0 <= (hi DOTMINUS lo) < grainSize then
                    CompactFullSeqScalarRange(lo,hi).generate[\T\](red,body)
                else
                    (* Identify power-of-2 boundary in region, split there *)
                    split = partitionL((lo BITXOR hi) DOTPLUS 1)
                    mid   = hi BITAND (BITNOT (split DOTMINUS 1))
                    red.join(loop'(lo,mid-1),loop'(mid,hi))

# What the transaction checks cost on the compiled path

Compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a `MutableFValue` cell. Before each read and each write of the cell, the generated code calls `BaseTask.inATransaction()`. For a local this is in `compiler/codegen/VarCodeGen.java:483-546`, for a field in `:620-726`. This note measures what share of a compiled loop's time these calls take today.

## 1. The answer

Each loop was timed in fresh JVMs, as a pair:
- "with checks" is the tree as it is;
- "without" has the checks removed by a shadow (§ 2).

How to read the table:
- Times are nanoseconds per loop iteration, or per element for TxArray.
- Each time is the median of 15 runs per variant, with the range (min-max) in brackets.
- "Pairs" is the difference inside each pair of runs, taken one after the other.
- All figures are for the third timed loop in each JVM, after the JIT's warm-up.

| program | with checks | without | difference | pairs | share | checks per iteration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TxScalar, the scalar loop | 20.42 (19.28-22.21) | 18.67 (16.42-19.99) | 1.75 | 1.96 (0.11-3.99) | 9 % | 2 |
| TxArray, the array loop | 23.17 (22.07-25.38) | 8.39 (8.17-9.05) | 14.79 | 14.60 (13.75-16.81) | 64 % | 7 |
| TxCell, the bare cell | 17.42 (16.30-19.04) | 14.56 (13.73-19.20) | 2.86 | 2.67 (-2.23-4.63) | 16 % | 2 |

- In the array loop, the checks take about two thirds of the time. Without them the loop runs 2.8 times as fast. The difference is far above the noise: every pair differs by 13.75 ns or more.
- In the scalar loop, the checks take about a tenth of the time. That difference is about as large as the spread between runs.
- One check costs about 2 ns in the array loop (14.79 / 7), and about 1 to 1.5 ns in the two scalar loops.
- The second timed loop shows the same:

content.content:
Abstract field declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{hidden}:}
A field declaration with the
modifier \KWD{hidden} has no implicit getter method.


\paragraph{\KWD{settable}:}
A field declaration with the modifier \KWD{settable} has an implicit
setter method unless there is an explicit setter declared in the enclosing
trait.  An implicit setter method takes a parameter
(with no default expression) whose type is the type of the field, and
returns \EXP{()}. When called, the implicit setter rebinds the
corresponding field to its argument.
If a field declaration includes the modifier  \KWD{settable} and
\KWD{hidden}, only an abstract setter is declared.
%
If a field declaration includes the modifier \KWD{hidden} without
\KWD{settable}, it is a static error.
If an abstract field declaration includes the modifier \KWD{settable},
it is mutable.
Because the \KWD{settable} modifier implies \KWD{var}, and
the \KWD{var} modifier without \KWD{settable} only affects implementations,
abstract field declarations do not include the \KWD{var} modifier.




\paragraph{\KWD{wrapped}:}
If a field declaration of $f$ has the modifier \KWD{wrapped}
and the type of $f$ is trait type $T$, and $T$ is not a naked type variable,
then the enclosing trait $S$ implicitly includes ``forwarding methods'' for
all methods in $T$ that are also inherited from any supertrait of $S$.
getter \VAR{spectralClass} of object \TYP{Sol}:



%Sol.spectralClass
\begin{Fortress}
\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass}\)
\end{Fortress}

If a field includes modifier \KWD{settable},
an implicit setter is defined for the
field. Calls to setters look like assignments.
Here is an assignment to field \VAR{spectralClass}
of object \TYP{Sol}:

%Sol.spectralClass := G3
\begin{Fortress}
\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass} \ASSIGN G_{3}\)
\end{Fortress}

In fact,
The type system and memory model in Fortress guarantee that an
\emph{initializing write} is performed to every location if it is ever read,
and that this write occurs before any read of the location.
Any location whose value can be written after initialization is
\emph{mutable}.  Mutable locations consist of
mutable variables and mutable fields of reference objects.
Any location whose value cannot be written after
initialization is \emph{immutable}.
Immutable locations are the non-\KWD{settable} immutable fields of a reference object.

An object declaration with the modifier \KWD{value} declares a value object
that is called in many languages a \emph{primitive} value.
The \objecttype\ declared by a value object implicitly has the modifier
\KWD{value}.



The fields of a \KWD{value} object are immutable;
they cannot be changed directly or it is a static error.
However, Fortress allows value objects to have settable fields
as an abbreviation for constructing a new value object with a different
value for one field.
If a value object has a setter method or a subscripted assignment operator
method (described in \secref{subscripted-assignment}),
then the return type of the method must be the value object trait type
instead of \EXP{()}.  When such a method is invoked, the receiver
must itself be assignable, and the value returned by the method
is assigned to the receiver.


For example, here is a value object \TYP{Complex} number:
%value object Complex(settable real:Double, settable imaginary:Double=0)
%  opr +(self,other:Complex) = Complex(real + other.real, imaginary + other.imaginary)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{value}\;\;\KWD{object} \TYP{Complex}(\KWD{settable} \VAR{real}\COLONOP\TYP{Double}, \KWD{settable} \VAR{imaginary}\COLONOP\TYP{Double}=0)\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{opr} +(\KWD{self},\VAR{other}\COLONOP\TYP{Complex}) = \TYP{Complex}(\VAR{real} + \VAR{other}.\VAR{real}, \VAR{imaginary} + \VAR{other}.\VAR{imaginary})\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
When a mutable variable \VAR{z}:
%var z : Complex = Complex(0)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{var} z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Complex} = \TYP{Complex}(0)\)
\end{Fortress}
updates its \VAR{imaginary} field, the following syntax:
%z.imaginary := v
\begin{Fortress}
\(z.\VAR{imaginary} \ASSIGN v\)
\end{Fortress}
can be used as an abbreviation for:
%z := Complex(z.real, v)
\begin{Fortress}
\(z \ASSIGN \TYP{Complex}(z.\VAR{real}, v)\)
\end{Fortress}
So the setter for the field \VAR{imaginary} in \TYP{Complex} would do the
work of constructing and returning

\section{Programming Discipline}
\seclabel{programmer-memory-model}

If Fortress programmers obey the following discipline, they can expect
sequentially consistent behavior from their Fortress programs:
\begin{itemize}

\item Updates to shared mutable locations must always be performed using an
  \KWD{atomic} expression.  A location is considered to be shared if
  and only if that location can be accessed by more than one thread at
  a time.  For example, statically partitioning an array among many
  threads need not make the array elements shared; only elements
  actually accessed by more than one thread are considered to be
  shared.

\item Within a thread or group of implicit threads objects must not
  be accessed through aliased references; this can yield unexpected
  results.  \secref{aliasing} defines the notion of \emph{apparently
    disjoint} references.  An object must not be written through one
  reference when it is accessed through another apparently disjoint
  reference.

\end{itemize}

The following stylistic guidelines reduce the possibility of
pathological behavior when a program strays from the above discipline:
\begin{itemize}

\item Where feasible, reduction must be used in favor of updating a
  single shared object.

\item Immutable fields and variables must be used wherever
  practical.  We discuss this further in \secref{immutability}.

\subsection{Reduction Variables}
\seclabel{reduction-vars}

\note{Reduction variables are not yet supported.}

To perform computations as locally as possible, and avoid the need to
synchronize in the middle of relatively simple \KWD{for} loops,
Fortress gives special treatment to \emph{reductions}.  We say that an
operator \EXP{\odot} is a \emph{reduction operator} for type $T$ if
$T$ is a subtype of
%Monoid[\T, ODOT\]
\(\TYP{Monoid}\llbracket{}T, \odot\rrbracket\), which implies that
\EXP{\odot} is an associative binary infix operator on $T$ (see
\secref{monoids-groups-rings-fields} for details about the
\TYP{Monoid} trait).

We say that a variable \VAR{l} is a \emph{reduction variable} reduced using
the reduction operator $\odot$ for a particular thread group if it
satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item Every assignment to \VAR{l} within the thread group is of the
  form \EXP{l \mathrel{\oplus}= e}, where exactly one operator $\oplus$ or its
  group inverse $\ominus$ (see below) is used in these assignments.
\item The value of \VAR{l} is not otherwise read within the thread group.
\item The variable \VAR{l} is not a free variable of a functional.
  This includes the fields of the receiver object in a method
  definition.
\end{itemize}
Other threads which simultaneously reference a reduction variable
while a loop is running may see an arbitrary value for that variable.
Any updates performed by those threads may be lost.  The association
of terms in the reduction is arbitrary and guided by the loop
generators (\secref{defining-generators}).  The order of terms in the
reduction is the natural order of elements in the generator.  When the
operator is commutative, the order of terms is also arbitrary.

Several common mathematical operators are declared to be monoids in
\library.  These include \EXP{+}, $\cdot$, \EXP{\wedge}, \EXP{\vee},
and \EXP{\xor}.  If a type $T$ extends
%Group[\T, OPLUS, OMINUS\]
\EXP{\TYP{Group}\llbracket{}T, \oplus, \ominus\rrbracket}
(see \secref{monoids-groups-rings-fields} for details about the
\TYP{Group} trait)
then reduction expressions of the following form are also permitted:
%x OMINUS= y
\begin{Fortress}
\(x \mathrel{\ominus}= y\)

content.content:
For some types, such as the integers \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} or the rationals \EXP{\mathbb{Q}},
results are always exact, and algebraic properties can be expected to be obeyed exactly.
For other types, such as floating-point numbers, results are not always numerically
exact, and algebraic properties can be expected to be obeyed only approximately.
For example, given three floating-point values \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} and \VAR{c},
it may well be that \EXP{a+(b+c)} is not equal to \EXP{(a+b)+c}; but we would expect
their values to be reasonably close---unless, of course, overflow occurred in one
expression but not the other.

In order to address the difficulties of such approximate computation,
many of the traits described in this section come in two varieties:
approximate and exact.  The \EXP{+} operator on integers or
rationals is correctly described by the trait \TYP{Associative}, and
the \EXP{+} operator on floating-point numbers is correctly described
by the trait \TYP{ApproximatelyAssociative}.  An important distinction
is that the predicate used to test acceptability of exact algebraic
properties is \EXP{=}, which is required to be an equivalence relation
and therefore transitive, but a type-dependent binary predicate
(typically \EXP{\approx}) may be used to test acceptability of
approximate algebraic properties, and this predicate is required only
to be reflexive and symmetric.

## 6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime

`variants/forkjoin/FlatArrays.java` gives the vocabulary's loops and sums the shape that the Fortress library and its compiled runtime give parallel work, on a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`. What a piece computes once it is no longer split is the baseline's plain loop, so its time is a floor for what compiled Fortress could reach with this structure and unboxed arrays.

| Shape | In the tree | In the variant |
|---|---|---|
| a parallel range | `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1310-1345`: a range of more than `grainSize` = 16 elements (`:20`) splits at the highest power-of-two boundary inside it; the two parts are the arms of a `do ... also do` | `forRange`, used by the model's row loops (`rows(rmsn)`, `rows(sm)`, ...), by `adam`'s loop over the 4,192 elements, by the loop over the planes and by the elementwise passes |
| a reduction | the same split, the two results joined; at most 16 elements fold left to right (`:1365-1373`) | `dot`, `sum`, `max`: no shared accumulator |
| the matrix product | `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`: the largest of the three dimensions is halved by `partition` (the largest power of two below it); the halves of the rows and of the columns are forked, the halves of the summed dimension run in sequence; it stops at one element | `mma`, under `mul`, `mulT`, `addMulT`, `tMul` and on each plane under the three `heads*` |
| the arms | `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1717-1770` and `runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`: every arm but the first becomes a task object; `forkIfProfitable` forks it if the pool has more than one thread and the worker's surplus of queued tasks is at most the spawn threshold (5, `FortressExecutable.java:26`); the first arm runs in place; `joinOrRun` joins the task or runs it in place | `Arm`: the same two methods; the program's body runs as a task of the pool |

Not given the shape: `gatherAdd`, `onehotTMul`, `addInto` and the elementwise loops written in `step` itself stay plain loops, and `onehotTMul` stays a scatter where the Fortress multiplies by a 0/1 matrix.

**Grains.** `baseline.grain` is the range's grain and `baseline.mmgrain` the product's: a product whose three dimensions are all at most that is one plain block. The library's own are 16 for the range and 1 for the product, which has no grain: it forks down to single elements. Timed: the library's (16, 1); (16, 16), the product given the range's grain, at which a 16x16x16 product is one block and only the 27 and 64 dimensions split; and (4, 4), finer, at which the model's sizes do split.

**The order of the sums against the plain loop.** The product's halving does not change it at any grain: the summed dimension is split in sequence. The range's halving changes every sum longer than the grain: at grain 16 the softmax sum over 27 logits, as in the library; at grain 4 every sum of 16 as well. Every configuration passes the 7 and the 40 checks (`./run.sh variants`: 9 configurations, threads 1, 2, 4 by the three grains).
